QUESTION PRESENTED
 In 2023, Washington State transferred the
responsibility to notify parents about certain runaway
youth from licensed homeless shelters to the state’s
child welfare agency, which also must offer voluntary
family reconciliation services and behavioral health
referrals to the youth and their family. Petitioners are
parents and organizations who challenged the revised
laws, basing their claim of injury on their worry that,
at some point in the future, their children might run
away, then might seek refuge with a licensed shelter,
then might decline reconciliation services, then might
accept a referral for behavior al health services, and
then might ultimately receive healthcare services
they oppose. Petitioners alleged that this potential
chain of events affected their parental rights, free
speech rights, and free exercise rights. The lower
courts dismissed this case for lack of Article III
standing, finding that the current harms Petitioners
alleged were self-imposed, and that the theoretical
chain of events Petitioners feared was too speculative
to show that the challenged laws have injured or will
likely injure them.
The question presented is:
 Whether Petitioners have standing to challenge
laws that impose no oblig ations on them based on
speculation that the laws may someday affect them?

ii

Ethical Care, Inc., Advocates Protecting Children, and
Parents 1A, 1B, 2A, 2B, 3A , 3B, 4A, 4B, 5A and 5B.

the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.

1



INTRODUCTION
 Petitioners are trying to sell this Court a bill
of goods. Their briefing misrepresents Washington
law and the facts here in critical ways. Even with
those misrepresentations, they  still have to ask this
Court to throw out black letter standing law to allow
their claims to proceed. The Court should decline their
request and either affirm th e lower courts or dismiss
this case as improvidently granted.
 Petitioners assert standing based on a chain of
speculation culminating in a lie about Washington
law. Their theory is that if one of their children:
(1) ran away (which none of the remaining plaintiffs
ever has); (2) ended up at a licensed youth homeless
shelter (same); and (3) sought gender-affirming care
(same again), then the State would provide their child
such care without informing them, creating incentives
for their children to run away.
 Setting aside the many speculative steps in
this chain, the whole premise is false because nothing
in the laws they challeng e allows the State to
provide gender-affirming care to runaway minors.
Under Washington law, if a minor runs away to a
licensed homeless shelter and is seeking genderaffirming care, the State offers the minor only contact
information for mental health providers, information
readily available online. The State does not pay
for any services, offer transportation to them, or
otherwise facilitate their provision in any way. The
idea that a minor would run away from home to obtain
information they could easily find online is ludicrous.
Not a single minor has made use of these laws to seek
gender-affirming care since their amendment in 2023.

2



 Given Petitioners’ misrepresentations and the
concession in their merits brief that nearly all of their
claims are moot, the simplest resolution here would be
to dismiss this case as improvidently granted. But if
the Court reaches the merits, it should affirm.
 This Court has long held that Article III
imposes three requirements for a plaintiff to have
standing: injury, causation, and redressability. Lujan
v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992). Most relevant
here, the plaintiff must show that their alleged injury
“is (a) concrete and particularized and (b) actual or
imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical.” Id. at 560
(citation modified).
 Petitioners fail this burden. They admit that
none of their children has invoked the laws they
challenge. They nonetheless claim that the laws
are currently harming them by causing them to alter
their “parenting styles” and what they say around
their children. This Court has routinely rejected
such arguments based on self-imposed changes in
behavior, see, e.g., Clapper v. Amnesty International
USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013), and if  changes in parental
behavior in reaction to hypothetical harm suffice to
show standing, then parents can sue about anything.
 Petitioners also assert that they will suffer
future injuries from the challenged laws, but there is
only one set of plaintiff parents left (2A and 2B) with
non-moot claims, and their allegations come nowhere
close to showing that these laws will ever affect them.
The theoretical possibility that their child could be the
first ever to use these laws as they fear fails to show
“actual or imminent” injury. Lujan, 504 U.S. at 560.

3



 Unable to satisfy this Court’s settled standing
test, Petitioners propose a new rule under which
anyone who is the “object” of a law can challenge it,
even without concrete or particularized harm. Setting
aside that Petitioners never raised this argument
below, it flies in the face of precedent. Indeed, the
United States as amicus curiae declines to endorse
this theory, and Petitioners’ own counsel in the
courts below filed an amicus brief here opposing this
theory. See Am. First Legal Found. Amicus Br. 25
(“[A]n ‘object’ of a challenged policy (whatever that
means) is not excused from his obligation to plead and
prove the components of Article III standing—injury
in fact, traceability, and redressability.”).
 While rejecting Petitioners’ novel, unworkable
theory, the United States offers its own: a special
standing rule only for substantive due process claims
based on parental rights. Under that theory, “parents
suffer an immediate, concrete, and cognizable harm as
soon as the government alters th[eir] authority[.]”
U.S. Amicus Br. 21-22. No court has ever endorsed
that rule, which would eviscerate standing doctrine.
The United States also ignores the need to define
the alleged substantive due process right at issue
with specificity. Most st ates have long allowed
some minors to consent to mental health treatment
(the only treatment at issue here) without parental
consent, and since the founding most States have
allowed minors to make even more consequential
decisions (such as whether to marry). Have all such
laws always been unconstitutional? The federal
government’s theory fails.
 This Court should affirm or dismiss.

4



STATEMENT
A. Homeless Youth Face Threats on the
Streets, Yet Often Avoid Licensed Shelters
 Hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied
youth experience homelessness each year. 1 Young
people experiencing homelessness are far more likely
than other youth to experience mental health and
substance abuse disorders, sexual exploitation,
trafficking, and other victimization.2
 LGBTQ+ youth are more than twice as likely to
experience homelessness as their heterosexual or
cisgender peers. 3 They experience particularly high
levels of adversity and victimization among homeless
youth, and are more likely to engage in survival sex or
be trafficked than non-LGBTQ+ youth.4


1 National Center for Homeless Education, Student
Homelessness in America: School Years 2017-18 to 2019-20
(2021), https://nche.ed.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/Student-
Homelessness-in-America-2021.pdf.
2 Thresia B. Gambon et al., Runaway Youth: Caring for
the Nation’s Largest Segment of Missing Children , 145
PEDIATRICS (2020).
3 Matthew H. Morton et al., Missed Opportunities:
LGBTQ Youth Homelessness in America , Chapin Hall at the
University of Chic ago (2018), https:// www.chapinhall.org/wpcontent/uploads/ChapinHall_VoYC_NationalReport_Final.pdf.
4 See The Trevor Project, Homelessness and Housing
Instability Among LGBTQ Youth  (2021), https://www.thetrevor
project.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Trevor-Project-Homeles
sness-Report.pdf.

5



 The vast majority of unaccompanied homeless
youth do not stay in licensed shelters, instead
staying temporarily with friends or extended family
or remaining unsheltered. 5 LGBTQ+ youth are
especially likely to end up on the streets.6
B. Washington Has Long Required Parental
Notification Regarding Runaway Youth,
With Multiple Avenues for Notification
 When a minor runs away from home, many
states have no law requiring parental notification. 7
Washington, however, has long required parental
notification, which can take a variety of forms.
 For decades, Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082
required homeless shelters to “report the location of
the child to the parent, the law enforcement agency
of the jurisdiction in which the person lives, or the
department [of children, youth, and families].” 1995
Wash. Sess. Laws, ch. 312, § 34(1) (emphasis added).
If the Department received such a report, it had to
“make a good faith attempt to notify the parent that a
report has been received and offer services designed
to resolve the conflict and accomplish a reunification
of the family.” 1996 Wash. Sess. Laws, ch. 133, § 14(3).


5 National Center for Homeless Education, supra note 2.
6 Id.
7 See, e.g. , Youth Homelessness Index, State Index on
Youth Homelessness  (Sept. 2025), https://perma.cc/J24E-KFNJ
(citing statutes).

6



 In 2013, the Legislature amended Wash. Rev.
Code § 13.32A.082 to distinguish licensed shelters
from other locations. Other locations remained subject
to the requirement to notify parents, law enforcement,
or the Department. But licensed shelters were now
required to notify a youth’s parents themselves
within seventy-two hours of the youth’s admission.
2013 Wash. Sess. Laws, ch. 4, § 2. The provision
made an exception, however, for “compelling reasons,”
including “circumstances that indicate that notifying
the parent or legal guardian will subject the minor to
abuse or neglect[.]” Id. In those instances, licensed
shelters were to notify the Department, which was
then required to notify parents and offer services to
help resolve the conflict. Id.
C. Washington Updated its Laws Regarding
Runaway Youth in 2023, Still Requiring
Parental Notification
 In 2023, the Legislature enacted Substitute
House Bill (SHB) 1406, 68th Leg., Reg. Sess.
(Wash. 2023), enacted as 2023 Wash. Sess. Laws,
ch. 151, and Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill
(ESSB) 5599, 68th Leg., Reg. Sess. (Wash. 2023),
enacted as 2023 Wash. Sess. Laws, ch. 408, further
amending Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082.
 SHB 1406 passed unanimously. It provides
that when a licensed shelter is unable to contact a
youth’s parent or the parent does not request their
child be returned home, the youth may stay in the
shelter for up to ninety days. 2023 Wash. Sess. Laws,
ch. 151, § 2. Before the amendment, youths whose
parents either could not be contacted or did not want

7



them home arguably had to be evicted after seventytwo hours. SHB 1406 fixed this problem. It also
provided that if a minor remains in a shelter under
these circumstances, the shelter must contact the
Department, which must offer family reconciliation
services within seventy-two hours. Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.32A.082(3)(a).
 ESSB 5599, meanwhile, encouraged youth
experiencing unsheltered homelessness to instead
engage with licensed shelters. See 2023 Wash.
Sess. Laws, ch. 408, § 1. The bill text and legislative
history recognized that many transgender youth
were choosing to remain on the streets instead
of accessing safer licensed shelters, and it attempted
to “remove barriers” to seeking licensed shelter
for those youth. Id.; see also  House Floor Debate
on ESSB 5599 (Wash. Apr. 12, 2023), at 2:32:07-
2:33:45, TVW, https://tvw.org/video/house-floordebate-april-12-2023041141/?eventID=2023041141
(Representative Cortes explaining that the bill will let
youth know “they have a safe place to go” and that one
barrier for some youth was fear that the shelter would
contact their parents).
 As part of this effort , the Legislature revised
parental notification requirements for licensed
shelters to return to a system more like what had been
in place for decades before the 2013 amendments.
Specifically, if a young person seeking reproductive
healthcare or gender-affirming care shows up to a
licensed youth shelter, the shelter must contact the
Department instead of contacting the youth’s parents
directly, just as the State allowed prior to 2013.
Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(1)(b)(i). Supra p. 6. The

8



Department must then attempt to notify parents,
offer family reconciliation services,8 and offer to make
referrals on behalf of the youth for behavioral health
services.9 Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(3)(a). Thus,
ESSB 5599 gives the Department an opportunity
to connect particularly vulnerable youth and
their families to additional, voluntary services. See
House Floor Debate at 48:03-48:55 (remarks of
Representative Rule: “We have an obligation to
protect [homeless youth] and to support them and
their families.”). As Representative Taylor put it:
“This bill is about bringing [Washington] kids home.”
House Floor Debate at 33:09-13.10
 As amended, Washington’s laws regarding
runaway minors still require more notice to parents
than many States, 11 including several of Petitioners’


8 “Family reconciliation se rvices” are “services . . .
designed to assess and stabilize the family with the goal of
resolving crisis.” Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.030(12).
9 “ ‘Behavioral health services’ means mental health
services, substance use disorder treatment services, and

§ 71.24.025(11).
10 Petitioners selectively quote Representative Taylor’s
remarks to mischaracterize her goal as “saving kids from their
parents by replacing parents with the State.” Pet’r’s.Br.10-11.
But Petitioners omit that she was referencing kids who have
been kicked out of their homes—whose parents tell them “you
cannot be here,” who “can’t go home,” and are “in the middle of
the cold.” House Floor Debate at 1:42:32-1:45:03. It is in these
circumstances that Representative Taylor insisted that the
Department “step in” to “provide a place for this child.” Id.
11 See Youth Homelessness Index, supra note 7.

9



amici, which allow shelters to notify a state agency
instead of parents in all cases,12 or require no parental
notification at all for some minors.13
 Nothing in the 2023 amendments permits
the Department to withhold any information from
parents. Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(3)(a) still
requires the Department to “make a good
faith attempt to notify” parents whenever it
receives a report of a runaway youth. To this
end, the Department’s memorandum implementing
ESSB 5599 instructs employ ees to “[m]ake [a] good
faith attempt to contact the youth’s parent or
legal guardian to offer [family reunification services,]”
and to “[d]ocument” the st eps they took to do
so. BIO.App.3a-4a. These good faith efforts
“must” include, “at minimum,” requesting contact
information from the youth or shelter and searching
the Department’s databas e “for any prior child
welfare history and contac t[ing] the most recent
contact information for a parent or legal guardian.” Id.
These minimum requirements generally exceed what
a licensed shelter can do because shelters lack access
to the Department’s database.
 Department policy also directs that its
“[c]aseworkers must . . . [c]o ntact the family within
twenty-four hours of being assigned the case,
excluding weekends and holidays, to schedule an
interview and assessment.” BIO.App.6a; see also
BIO.App.2a. Thus, the Department generally requires

12 See, e.g. , Alaska Stat. § 47.10.394; Utah Code
§ 80-5-602.
13 See, e.g., Tex. Fam. Code §§ 32.201, .202, .203.

10



parental notification within the same 24-72-hour
period previously applicable to licensed shelters.
See Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(1)(b)(i). And Wash.
Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(5) ex plicitly provides that
“[n]othing in this section prohibits any person . . . from
immediately reporting the identity and location of
any minor . . . more promptly than required under
this section.”
 These notice requirements dovetail with other
notice requirements throughout Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.32A.082 and related laws. See Pet.App.5a-6a.
For example, the requirement that the Department
“[o]ffer services desi gned to . . . accomplish a
reunification of the family[,]” Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.32A.082(3)(b)(ii), necessarily requires the
Department to notify the minor’s parents. Moreover,
Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(1)(b)(ii) continues
to require shelters to check the Washington State
Patrol’s missing children database “[a]t least once
every eight hours” and notify the Department
“immediately” if a minor in the shelter has been
reported missing—regardless of whether that minor
is seeking protected healthcare.
 The law does not require (or permit)
the Department to “den[y]” parents “information
about their child’s location or condition.” Contra
Pet’r’s.Br.13. Rather, the Department may only
withhold information about a minor’s whereabouts
and condition if it determines “that release of this
information is likely to cause severe psychological
or physical harm to the juvenile[.]” Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.50.100(7)(a). Thus, as amended, Washington’s
law does not deny any information to parents,
it merely changes who notifies the parents—the

11



Department as opposed to a licensed shelter—giving
the Department an opportunity to offer services to
vulnerable youth and their families to hopefully begin
a reunification process.
 Nothing in the 2023 laws authorizes the
Department to take custody of a minor. Contra
Pet’rs’.Br.14. When the Department notifies a
parent—as required by law—that their child is
in a licensed shelter, the parent is free to pick up
their child immediately. This is true regardless of
whether the youth or their parents choose to engage
in services offered by the Department. Contra
Pet’rs’.Br.14-15. Under long-established Washington
law, the Department may on ly take custody of a
minor where a court finds “that there are reasonable
grounds to believe that removal is necessary to
prevent imminent physical harm to the child due
to child abuse or neglect[.]” Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.34.050; see Wash. Rev. Code § 13.34.060(1).
 Washington law also does not “‘treat[] the
parents of children suffering from gender dysphoria
as per se neglectful or abusive[.]’” Contra Pet’rs’.Br.6
(quoting Pet.App.38a). Abusive and neglectful parents
can be temporarily denied information about their
children’s whereabouts and even lose custody. Supra
pp. 10-11. Not so for parent s whose kids are seeking
protected health care.

12



D. Nothing in Washington’s Revised Laws
Allows the State to Provide Gender-
Affirming Care to Runaway Minors
 Nothing in the laws at issue here permits
the Department to provide gender-affirming care
to minors. As amended, the law merely requires
the Department to offer voluntary referrals for
“behavioral health services.” Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.32A.082(3)(b). “‘Behavioral health services’
means mental health services, substance use
disorder treatment services, and co-occurring
disorder treatment services . . . .” Wash. Rev. Code
§ 71.24.025(11). It does not include medical services
like puberty blockers or hormone replacement
therapy. Id. And “referrals” simply means information
about services—information that is already available
to anyone with an internet browser. See Wash.
State Dep’t of Children, Youth & Families,  Mental
Health Referral Service for Children and Teens ,
https://perma.cc/AR8M-VGGY (last visited Oct. 18,
2026). Nothing more.
 Even as to “behavioral health services,” the
law does not require or allow the Department to
provide such services, contact providers, schedule
appointments, or pay for any services. See Wash.
Rev. Code § 13.34.315 (the Department may only
“authorize . . . routine and necessary medical, dental,
or mental health care” when “a child is ordered
removed from his or her home” by a court). And
nothing in either law restricts parents’ input in
decision-making or compels treatment for youth.

13



 Thus, nothing in either 2023 law changes
minors’ access to gender-affirming care, as even
the law’s opponents admit. See, e.g. , Senate Floor
Debate on ESSB 5599 (Wash. Mar. 1, 2023),
at 1:12:26-1:12:32, TVW, https://tvw.org/video/senatefloor-debate-march-1-2023031100/?eventID=2023031
100 (Senator Braun, Republican Minority Leader,
saying: “[T]his underlying bill . . . isn’t about access to
this care, which wouldn’t change with this
amendment.”).
 In short, the amendments simply alter who
notifies parents when youth end up at licensed
shelters and requires the Department to offer services
to youth and their families (which they can accept or
reject).
E. Washington’s Revised Notification Laws
Have Never Been Used
 In the more than three years since SHB 1406
and ESSB 5599 passed, lice nsed shelters have
contacted the Department zero times  about a
runaway youth seeking gender-affirming care or
pregnancy care. See Wash. State Dep’t of Children,
Youth & Families, Licensed Homeless Shelters ,
https://perma.cc/SSQ3-RTEA (last visited Oct. 18,
2026). For context, the Department received over 185
calls from licensed shelters during this period about
other situations requiring notice to the Department,
such as abuse or neglect. Id.

14



F. Washington’s Age of Consent Law for
Outpatient Mental Health Services
 Petitioners also challenge Wash. Rev. Code
§ 71.34.530 insofar as they contend it interacts with
ESSB 5599 to afford runaway youths a pathway to
receive gender-affirming care. See Pet’rs’.Br.12, 40.
 Wash. Rev. Code § 71.34.530 allows adolescents
thirteen and older to “request and receive outpatient
[behavioral health] treatment without the consent of
the adolescent’s parent.” Wash. Rev. Code § 71.34.530;
see also Wash. Rev. Code § 71.34.020(46) (defining
“outpatient treatment” to include only behavioral
health treatment). But it does not permit minors to
consent to medical care like puberty blockers or
hormone replacement therapy.  And it does not block
parents from accessing records about their children’s
care. Washington law allows  providers to disclose
“all information and records related to mental health
services” to a “minor’s parent.” Wash. Rev. Code
§ 70.02.240; see also Wash. Rev. Code § 71.34.430
(permitting providers to “release mental health
information about an adoles cent to a parent of the
adolescent without the consent of the adolescent”).
 Washington passed this law in 1985, toward
the tail end of a decades-long trend by States to permit
minors to consent to mental health care and health
care more generally. Idaho passed the first such law
in 1951, permitting minors as young as fourteen to
consent to mental health hospitalization. Hannah L.
Brown et al., History of Minor Consent Laws for
Mental Health Treatment in the US , JAMA HEALTH
FORUM (Apr. 24, 2026), https://jamanetwork.com/
journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2847947. In

15



1956, Rhode Island became the first state to pass a
statute permitting minors to consent to health care
more generally. Id. And over the next three decades—
as this Court was recognizing minors’ rights in cases
like In re Gault, 387 U.S. 1 (1967), and Goss v. Lopez,
419 U.S. 565 (1975)—dozens of  states passed similar
laws. Today, over thirty-five states allow minors to
consent to mental health care in some form, including

ever “take[] advantage of the state-revised regime.”
Id. at 4, 24. The federal government describes this as

(free speech); Harris, 448 U.S. at 321 & n.24 (free
exercise); Hays, 515 U.S. at 745 (equal protection).
And why would this relaxed standing policy be limited
to parents’ claims about medical decisions as opposed
to other decisions parents historically controlled, such
as educational ones? Or would the federal government
also allow parents to sue about educational policies
they opposed, even if they had no effect on their own
children? The federal government cannot say.
 Additionally, the federal government’s theory
of special standing for substantive due process claims
engages in the same sort of broad generalizations
about substantive due proces s rights that this Court
has long criticized. See Dobbs, 597 U.S. at 239-40;
Washington v. Glucksberg , 521 U.S. 702, 721 (1997)
(citing cases). The premise of the government’s theory
is that a parent historically had complete “authority
over his or her child, and with that the right to control
the entire process of deliberation [about medical
decisions]—from the discussions leading up to a
medical decision, to the permission culminating in the
decision itself.” U.S. Amicus Br. 3. But this Court has
never held that, and it is demonstrably false.
 The primary case the United States cites for
this theory is Parham v. J. R. , 442 U.S. 584 (1979),
but while that case certainly recognized that parents
have a “substantial, if not the dominant, role” in their
children’s medical decisions, it also said that such
decisions are still subject to “prerogatives of the child”

53



as well as input from physicians and the State’s
“significant interest.” Id. at 604. And while Mirabelli
recognized (in an emergency order) the likely
existence of a parental “right not to be shut out of
participation in decisions regarding their children’s
mental health,” 607 U.S. at 497 (emphasis added),
that is a far cry from “the right to control the entire
process of deliberation” the federal government
asserts here. U.S. Amicus Br. 3. Even the “right not to
be shut out” must be cabined in some way if it is to be
rooted in historical practice rather than present-day
policy concerns, because at the founding minors could
often make major health decisions without parental
consent. For example, mino rs as young as fourteen
could marry, e.g., Parton v. Hervey , 67 Mass. 119,
121-23 (1854), and then have  children, with all
the serious health risks attendant to that decision. If
parents could not dictate those decisions then, why
can they now?
 The federal government’s off-the-cuff
substantive due process theory could also have
profound consequences if accepted. Three dozen states
allow some minors to consent to various types of
health care, especially mental health care, without
parental approval. Supra pp. 14-15. Are those
statutes all unconstitutional? Relatedly, if States
cannot “restrict[] parents’ control over the medical
care their child may access,” U.S. Amicus Br. 4, it is
hard to understand under the federal government’s
theory how States could deny minors access to
abortion or gender-affirming care if their parents
wanted it for them.

54



 All of this is to say that it would be
extraordinarily risky for this Court to adopt a new
parental standing theory here that no court has ever
endorsed, that has not been  tested in lower courts,
that is presented only in an amicus brief, and that
could have far-reaching implications.
 The federal government counters that rejecting
its proposed rule would “create a jurisprudence of
chaos,” lead to endless emergency litigation, and
require impossible inquiries. U.S. Amicus Br. 4, 26.
But the federal government seems to forget that it is
the one asking for a new rule; for decades, this Court
has required particularized, concrete, and actual
harm, and the problems the United States alleges
have not materialized.
 At bottom, by limiting who can sue to those
with concrete and particularized injuries, standing
implements “the Framers’ concept of the proper—and
properly limited—role of the courts in a democratic
society.” All. for Hippocratic Med. , 602 U.S. at 380
(quoting J. Roberts,  Article III Limits on Statutory
Standing, 42 D UKE L. J. 1219, 1220 (1993)). But the
federal government’s relaxed standing test would
permit parents who have policy objections but no
concrete injury to sue and force courts “‘to rule on
important constitutional issues in the abstract[.]’”
Hein v. Freedom From Religion Found., Inc., 551 U.S.
587, 635-36 (2007) (Scalia, J., concurring in judgment)
(citation omitted). The Court should decline that
invitation.

55

The Court should dismiss this case as
improvidently granted or affirm the judgment below.
